place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 外门 · 执事房前
place.en: Chending Temple · The outer court · the steward's door

setup.zh: 九月初十，天没亮，饭堂门口排起了长龙：周衡发腰牌、灵石，马小宝收公中。身后有人拍你肩膀——阿禾。
setup.en: The tenth of the ninth month, before dawn, a long queue at the refectory door: Zhou Heng hands out waist tags and spirit stones, Ma Xiaobao collects the common fund. Someone taps your shoulder from behind — Ah He.

recap.zh: 入门第二天，阿禾也在——考进来的，三灵根，「中上之资」；她在小本子上记了你一笔：下下之资，利息以后再算。
recap.en: Your second day in the sect, Ah He was there too — passed on merit, three roots, "above the middle"; she wrote you into her notebook: bottom of the bottom, interest reckoned later.

zh: 九月初十，执事房前，领灵石，交公中。
身后有人拍你的肩膀——一个红鼻头。
en: The tenth of the ninth month: draw stones, pay the common fund.
Someone taps your shoulder — a red nose.

story.zh:
饭堂门口摆一张榆木桌子，桌子后面坐着外门执事周衡。周衡是个三十来岁的瘦高个儿，一脸愁苦，面前摊着一本厚得能当枕头使的账簿，叫一个名字，发两样东西：一块腰牌，三块灵石。腰牌是枣木的，巴掌大，一面刻「沉鼎」，一面刻各人的名字。那灵石有鸽子蛋大小，灰扑扑的，里头却隐隐透出一点光来，像雪地里埋着的一粒火星。领到的人捧在手心里，翻来覆去地瞧，瞧完了往怀里一揣，又忍不住掏出来再瞧，倒像怕它长了腿跑掉。

周衡发一个人，便在账簿上记一笔，记一笔，便抬头看那人一眼，道一声：「有前途！」发给真灵根的，他说「有前途！」；发给四灵根色杂的，他也说「有前途！」；发到第三十几个，那三个字已经说得像念经，前头的「有」字给吞了一半，只剩「前途」两个字从嘴角漏出来。轮到马小宝，周衡看了看名册上「荐书」那两个字，嘴唇动了一动，那三个字到底没说出口。轮到小满，他看了看名册上「五行杂灵根」那几个字，抬起头来，端详了小满好一会儿，道：「……有前途。」没有那个叹号。

小满捧着那块腰牌，又隔着衣裳摸了摸胸口那块狐纹木牌，忍不住笑了一笑。他进山的时候，胸口挂一块木牌；进了山门，腰上又挂一块木牌。一块是给他发灵石的，一块是欠他一张饼的。两块都是木头，两块他都得好好收着。

掌勺的是个胖大娘，一人一勺糙米粥，一碟咸菜，一只粗瓷碗。一百来个孩子扑到长桌跟前，稀里呼噜，满屋子都是喝粥的声音，倒像下了一场急雨。小满一碗粥喝完了，把碗捧起来，把碗底舔得干干净净，这才放下。放下了，他又拿起来。那是一只粗瓷碗，灰白的，碗口上一道青边，饭堂里这样的碗，少说也有两三百只。可这一只，碗沿上一个缺口也没有。

小满捧着它，看了很久。他想起家里那四只碗，想起碎在地上的那七八片，想起他娘蹲在地上，一片一片地捡，捡起来拿布包好，放进箱子里。胖大娘过来收碗，见他还捧着一只空碗发呆，便道：「还要？没了。一人一勺。」小满道：「不要了。」他把碗递过去，递到一半，又道：「大娘，这碗……明天还是这一只么？」那大娘看傻子似的看了他一眼，道：「碗还分这一只那一只？」一把夺了过去，丢进木盆里，「哗啦」一声，跟两三百只碗混在了一处。

身后忽然有人拍他肩膀。

小满回头一看，是一个扎两根小辫子的姑娘，穿着一身跟他一样的灰袍，却比他的还大一号，袖子挽了三道，下摆拿草绳在腰里扎了一圈，才不至于拖地。一个红鼻头，冻得像一根萝卜。手里捏着一个巴掌大的小本子，一截炭条夹在耳朵上。

小满瞧着她，觉得面熟。这张脸他昨天在石阶上见过，在石坪上见过，在正殿里测灵石的时候也见过，每一回都只见着一个后脑勺，一截小辫子一晃，便给人群挡住了。他那时候心想，这世上红鼻头的姑娘多了，石坳村的阿禾，她娘连村口都不让她出，怎么会跑到三百里外的泗水来？

他又瞧了一眼。那姑娘也瞧着他，一声不吭，只从耳朵上取下那截炭条，在小本子上写了一个字。

小满张大了嘴，半晌，才道：「……阿禾？」

阿禾道：「嗯。」

「你怎么在这？」

「考进来的。」

「你——你昨天就在？」

「前天就在。」阿禾道，「石阶上，我从你边上冲过去的。洛书，我比你先摆好半炷香。测灵石，我排在你前头第三个。」她顿了一顿，一本正经地道，「你三回都没认出我。」

小满脸上一热，忙道：「我认出来了！我就是……没敢认。」

阿禾把小本子翻开来，指着刚写的那一行给他看。那一行写的是：**九月初十。认出。三回半。**

小满问：「半回是什么？」

阿禾道：「方才你瞧了我两眼，头一眼没认出来，第二眼才认出来，算半回。」

小满没话说了，只好换个问题：「你怎么没跟我一起来？」

阿禾道：「我娘说，你一个人去，会死。我一个人去，也会死。两个人一起去，死一双，不划算。所以分开走。」

小满听得发怔：「……这是什么道理？」

阿禾道：「风险分散。」

小满想了一想，觉得这话虽然难听，账倒是算得明白。他娘说过，阿禾她娘是石坳村第二会算账的人，第一是她自己。

他又问：「你什么灵根？」

阿禾面无表情地道：「三灵根。真灵根。执事说我『中上之资』。」

小满张了张嘴，半个字也没说出来。昨天测灵石的时候，殿里一阵惊叹，他踮起脚来想看是谁，只看见一截小辫子——原来那一阵惊叹，是给阿禾的。

阿禾反问：「你呢？」

她明明是知道的。那时候她排在他前头第三个，测完了就站在殿柱子底下，满殿的人笑成一锅粥，她是没笑的那两个里头的一个。可她偏要问，问得一本正经，像是非得从他嘴里听一遍，才算数。

小满也面无表情地道：「五灵根。五行杂灵根。执事说我『下下之资』。」

阿禾看了他一会儿，舔了舔炭条，在本子上又写了一行。小满伸长脖子问：「写什么呢？」阿禾念道：「『九月初十。沈小满。下下之资。』」念罢合上本子，「利息，以后再算。」
story.en:
At the refectory door stood an elm table, and behind it sat the outer court's steward, Zhou Heng. Zhou Heng was a tall, thin man of about thirty with a woeful face; spread before him was a ledger thick enough to use as a pillow, and as he called each name he handed out two things: a waist tag and three spirit stones. The tag was jujube wood, palm-sized, carved "Chending" on one face and the disciple's name on the other. The spirit stones were the size of pigeon eggs, dusty grey, yet a faint light showed inside, like a spark buried in snow. Those who got them held them in their palms and turned them over and over, tucked them inside their jackets, then couldn't help taking them out to look again, as if afraid they'd grow legs and run.

For each one Zhou Heng made an entry in the ledger, and for each entry he looked up at the person and said: "A future!" To a true root he said "A future!"; to a four-root, colours mixed, he also said "A future!"; by the thirtieth-odd the words had gone like a sutra chant, the first swallowed, only "…future" leaking from the corner of his mouth. At Ma Xiaobao he looked at the words "letter of recommendation" in the register, his lips moved, and the words never came out. At Xiaoman he looked at "mixed five-element root" in the register, looked up, studied Xiaoman a good while, and said: "…A future." Without the exclamation mark.

Xiaoman held the waist tag, and through his clothes felt the fox-patterned token on his chest, and couldn't help smiling. He had come to the mountain with a wooden token on his chest; through the gate, he had another wooden token on his waist. One paid him spirit stones; one owed him a flatbread. Both were wood, and both he'd have to keep carefully.

The cook was a stout auntie: a ladle of coarse rice gruel each, a dish of pickles, a coarse clay bowl. A hundred-odd children fell on the long tables, slurping, the whole room full of the sound of gruel, like a sudden downpour. Xiaoman finished his bowl, lifted it, and licked the bottom clean before setting it down. Set it down, and picked it up again. It was a coarse clay bowl, greyish white, a green line round the rim — the refectory had two or three hundred bowls like it at least. But this one had not a single chip on its rim.

Xiaoman held it and looked at it a long time. He thought of the four bowls at home, the seven or eight pieces on the floor, his mother squatting to pick them up one by one, wrapping them in cloth, putting them in the chest. The stout auntie came to collect the bowls, saw him still holding an empty bowl and staring, and said: "More? None left. One ladle each." Xiaoman said, "No more." He handed the bowl over, and halfway, said: "Auntie, this bowl… will it be this one again tomorrow?" The auntie looked at him as at a simpleton. "Bowls are this one and that one now?" She snatched it, tossed it in the wooden tub — *crash* — and it was lost among two or three hundred bowls.

Someone tapped him on the shoulder from behind.

Xiaoman turned. It was a girl with two little braids, in the same grey robe as his, only a size bigger still, the sleeves rolled up three times and the hem tied round her waist with a straw rope so it wouldn't drag. A red nose, frozen like a radish. In her hand a notebook no bigger than a palm; a stick of charcoal tucked behind her ear.

Xiaoman looked at her and thought the face familiar. He had seen it yesterday on the stone steps, on the stone terrace, and in the hall at the root-testing too — each time only the back of a head, the flick of a braid, and then the crowd closed over it. He had told himself at the time that the world was full of girls with red noses; Ah He of Stone Hollow, whose mother wouldn't let her past the village gate, could hardly have turned up at the Si, three hundred li away.

He looked again. The girl looked back at him without a word, took the charcoal from behind her ear, and wrote one character in the notebook.

Xiaoman's mouth fell open. At last he said, "…Ah He?"

"Mm," said Ah He.

"What are you doing here?"

"Passed the test."

"You — you were here yesterday?"

"The day before," said Ah He. "On the steps I ran right past you. On the Luo diagram I was done half a stick of incense before you. At the testing stone I was three ahead of you in the line." She paused, and said in all seriousness, "Three times you didn't recognise me."

Xiaoman's face went hot. "I did recognise you! I just… didn't dare."

Ah He opened the notebook and showed him the line she had just written: **Ninth month, tenth day. Recognised. Three and a half times.**

"What's the half?" Xiaoman asked.

"Just now you looked at me twice. The first look you didn't know me, the second you did. That's a half."

Xiaoman had nothing to say to that, so he tried another question. "Why didn't you come with me?"

"My mother said if you go alone, you'll die. If I go alone, I'll die too. Two going together and dying as a pair — bad bargain. So we split up."

Xiaoman stared. "…What kind of reasoning is that?"

"Spreading the risk," said Ah He.

Xiaoman thought it over; ugly as it sounded, the sum was right. His mother had once said that Ah He's mother was the second-best reckoner in Stone Hollow — the best being herself.

He asked, "What roots have you got?"

Ah He said, without expression, "Three roots. A true root. The steward says I'm 'above the middle.'"

Xiaoman opened his mouth and not half a word came out. Yesterday at the testing stone a gasp had gone round the hall and he had stood on tiptoe to see who it was, and seen only a braid — so that gasp had been for Ah He.

"And you?" Ah He asked back.

She knew perfectly well. She had been three ahead of him; after her test she had stood under a pillar of the hall, and when the whole hall laughed itself into porridge she had been one of the two who didn't laugh. But she asked anyway, quite solemnly, as if it only counted once she'd heard it from his own mouth.

Xiaoman said, just as expressionless, "Five roots. Mixed five-element roots. The steward says I'm 'the bottom of the bottom.'"

Ah He looked at him for a while, licked her charcoal, and wrote another line. Xiaoman craned his neck. "What are you writing?" Ah He read it out: "'Ninth month, tenth day. Shen Xiaoman. Bottom of the bottom.'" Then she shut the notebook. "Interest — reckoned later."

exits.means: accepts Ah He's entry, lets the interest stand, goes on to the lesson

what.zh: 外门第一天，阿禾在小本子上记了你一笔：下下之资。利息，以后再算。
what.en: Your first day in the outer court: Ah He wrote you into the little notebook — bottom of the class. Interest to be reckoned later.

story.zh:
小满想了一想，道：「记吧。利息，我认。」

阿禾点了点头，像是他总算说了一句像样的话。她转身要走，走了两步，又回过头来，补了一句：「鸡蛋，三个半。别忘了。」

小满站在原地，瞧着她那两截小辫子一跳一跳地走远了，心里头说不出是什么滋味。他想起出门那天，老槐树底下只站着他娘一个人。他那时候还道这丫头在睡懒觉。

原来她早走了一天，走的是另一条路。
story.en:
Xiaoman thought it over and said, "Write it down. The interest — I'll own it."

Ah He nodded, as if he had finally said something sensible. She turned to go, took two steps, looked back and added, "Eggs: three and a half. Don't forget."

Xiaoman stood where he was and watched her two little braids bob away, and could not have said what he felt. He remembered the day he left: under the old locust tree there had been only his mother. He had supposed the girl was sleeping in.

So she had gone a day early, by another road.

exits.means: argues about the interest, refuses to own the debt

what.zh: 外门第一天，阿禾在小本子上记了你一笔：下下之资。你不认账——利息翻倍。
what.en: Your first day in the outer court: Ah He wrote you into the little notebook — bottom of the class. You disowned the debt, so the interest doubled.

story.zh:
小满道：「这也要算利息？」

阿禾道：「什么都要算利息。」她转身要走，走了两步，又回过头来，补了一句，「鸡蛋，三个半。别忘了。」

小满站在原地，瞧着她那两截小辫子一跳一跳地走远了，心里头说不出是什么滋味。他想起出门那天，老槐树底下只站着他娘一个人。他那时候还道这丫头在睡懒觉。

原来她早走了一天，走的是另一条路。
story.en:
"Even this earns interest?" said Xiaoman.

"Everything earns interest," said Ah He. She turned to go, took two steps, looked back and added, "Eggs: three and a half. Don't forget."

Xiaoman stood where he was and watched her two little braids bob away, and could not have said what he felt. He remembered the day he left: under the old locust tree there had been only his mother. He had supposed the girl was sleeping in.

So she had gone a day early, by another road.
